nodes.label: Interleaved Practice
nodes.description: Mixing problem types within a session instead of blocking them. Performance during practice drops; retention and transfer rise.
nodes.why: Blocked practice teaches you to execute a method; interleaving teaches you to choose one.

evidence.measurementMethod: Performance on a mixed test containing problem types you did not know were coming, taken at least a day after practice.
evidence.knownLimitations: Interleaving reliably feels worse and works better. It slows within-session performance, which makes adherence the real difficulty.

nodes.label: Method of Loci
nodes.description: Hanging arbitrary information on a vividly imagined route through a familiar place, exploiting how durable spatial memory is.
nodes.why: It converts material your memory ignores into material it is built to hold.

evidence.measurementMethod: Ordered recall of an unseen list after a fixed encoding time, retested a week later.
evidence.knownLimitations: Mnemonic training produces dramatic, well-replicated gains on the trained list-learning task and does not raise general memory ability.

nodes.label: Knowledge System
nodes.description: An external store with real linking, so that past thinking is retrievable and can collide productively with new material. An unindexed archive is not a knowledge system.
nodes.why: Memory is lossy and associative; a linked external store is the prosthesis that makes long-term synthesis possible.

evidence.measurementMethod: Retrieval success: how often you find the note you needed at the moment you needed it, counted rather than estimated.
evidence.knownLimitations: Note systems are widely evangelised on almost no controlled evidence. A system that is never read is an expensive filing habit.

nodes.label: Mental Model Library
nodes.description: A stocked, cross-disciplinary set of explanatory frames — feedback, incentives, selection, compounding — with a clear sense of where each applies.
nodes.why: A broad model library is what lets you recognise a familiar structure inside an unfamiliar problem.

evidence.measurementMethod: Apply a named model to an unseen case and state what it predicts that the obvious analysis does not.
evidence.knownLimitations: Collections of named models are easy to accumulate and hard to apply. Without a prediction step this becomes vocabulary, not understanding.

nodes.label: Knowledge Breadth
nodes.description: Deliberate sampling well outside your specialisation, at enough depth to recognise the structure rather than just the vocabulary.
nodes.why: Breadth is what supplies the source domains that analogical transfer draws on.

evidence.measurementMethod: Unaided explanation of core ideas from fields outside your own, checked against a source afterwards.
evidence.knownLimitations: Breadth supports comprehension and analogy, but broad shallow knowledge is routinely mistaken for understanding, especially by its holder.

nodes.label: Domain Depth
nodes.description: Going deep enough in one field to hold expert-level chunks and to have opinions that survive contact with practitioners.
nodes.why: Depth in one domain is what teaches you what real understanding feels like, so you can recognise its absence elsewhere.

evidence.measurementMethod: Performance on representative domain tasks at professional difficulty, and the ability to recognise what you do not know within the domain.
evidence.knownLimitations: Depth is the single strongest predictor of performance within a domain and one of the weakest predictors outside it.

nodes.label: Transfer
nodes.description: Actually deploying knowledge in a context unlike the one you learned it in — which happens far less automatically than education assumes.
nodes.why: Knowledge that never transfers is inert, and most of it stays inert unless transfer is practised on purpose.

evidence.measurementMethod: Documented instances where something learned in one context solved a problem in a genuinely different one — recorded at the time, not recalled.
evidence.knownLimitations: Far transfer is rare and hard to produce deliberately. Neuron tracks it because it is the honest bar, not because it expects it often.

nodes.label: Quantitative Literacy
nodes.description: Reading numbers critically: units, denominators, distributions, and what a statistic is silently leaving out.
nodes.why: Most numeric claims that mislead are technically true, and only the denominator gives them away.

evidence.measurementMethod: Interpret an unseen statistic, chart or risk claim correctly, including stating what is missing from it.
evidence.knownLimitations: Statistical fluency is domain-transferable more than most knowledge, but it does not immunise anyone against motivated reasoning on topics they care about.

nodes.label: Historical Context
nodes.description: Knowing how the present arrangement came about, and therefore which parts of it are contingent rather than inevitable.
nodes.why: Without history, every current arrangement looks like the only one that was ever possible.

evidence.measurementMethod: Explain a current situation's antecedents unaided, and name the counterexample that complicates your own account.
evidence.knownLimitations: Historical analogy is persuasive and frequently misleading. Superficial similarity between events is the default failure mode.

nodes.label: Technical Fluency
nodes.description: Enough command of your tools that they stop competing for attention with the problem you are using them on.
nodes.why: Tool friction is a working-memory tax you pay on every single session until you remove it.

evidence.measurementMethod: Read unfamiliar technical material in the domain and correctly state what it does and where it would fail.
evidence.knownLimitations: Technical vocabularies age fast. Fluency in a stack is a perishable asset, not a durable cognitive gain.

nodes.label: Goal Maintenance
nodes.description: Keeping an active goal represented and dominant while you work, so that what you are doing at minute forty is still what you decided to do at minute one. It is the difference between being distracted and having quietly forgotten the point.
nodes.why: Almost every failure people call 'procrastination' or 'distraction' is a goal that stopped being represented. Restoring the goal is cheaper than restoring the motivation.

evidence.measurementMethod: Interrupt yourself at random intervals and write down, unprompted, the goal you believe you are currently pursuing. Score the match against the goal you wrote at the start of the block.
evidence.knownLimitations: Goal maintenance is measurable in the lab (AX-CPT and similar) but the everyday version depends heavily on environment and sleep. Improvement here is often environmental redesign rather than a capacity change.

nodes.label: Response Inhibition
nodes.description: Cancelling a prepared response before it executes — the hand already moving to the phone, the reply already forming. Distinct from working-memory updating: this is stopping, not revising.
nodes.why: The gap between having an impulse and emitting it is where almost all of your leverage over your own behaviour lives.

evidence.measurementMethod: Stop-signal reaction time in a go/no-go task, plus a real-world count: intended-versus-emitted responses in one situation you nominate in advance.
evidence.knownLimitations: Laboratory inhibition correlates only weakly with everyday self-control, and training the lab task moves the lab task. Do not read a better stop-signal score as better restraint.

nodes.label: Cognitive Flexibility
nodes.description: Switching between task sets, rules or framings on demand, and paying as little as possible for the switch. Includes the harder half: abandoning a rule that used to work.
nodes.why: Rigidity is expensive precisely when the situation has changed — which is exactly when you are least likely to notice.

evidence.measurementMethod: Switch cost: your accuracy and response time on switch trials minus repeat trials in a task-switching probe. Real-world proxy: time from evidence-of-change to strategy-change.
evidence.knownLimitations: Switch costs are robust and trainable within a paradigm, with little evidence of generalisation. High flexibility also has a cost — it trades against goal maintenance.

nodes.label: Planning & Sequencing
nodes.description: Turning an intention into an ordered set of actions with dependencies, and doing the ordering before you start rather than discovering it halfway through.
nodes.why: Most plans fail at the seams — the step nobody sequenced. Explicit ordering surfaces the dependency you would otherwise hit at the worst moment.

evidence.measurementMethod: Plan-versus-actual: the number of steps you had to reorder or insert during execution, and the ratio of estimated to actual duration.

nodes.label: Task Initiation
nodes.description: Starting, specifically: closing the gap between deciding to do something and the first real action on it. The failure mode is not laziness but an under-specified first step.
nodes.why: Initiation latency is where the largest share of intended work is actually lost, and it responds to structural fixes far better than to resolve.

nodes.label: Error Monitoring
nodes.description: Detecting that you have just made an error — ideally before the consequence arrives, and without needing someone else to point it out. Includes noticing the felt signal of a mistake and acting on it rather than continuing.
nodes.why: An undetected error compounds. The interval between making a mistake and noticing it is one of the few quantities that improves nearly everything downstream when it shrinks.

evidence.measurementMethod: Self-caught error rate: of the errors eventually found in your work, what share did you catch yourself, and how long after committing them?
evidence.knownLimitations: Error-related brain responses are well established; deliberately training error awareness in everyday work is not. Checking more can also mean finishing less.

nodes.description: Judging how much a given piece of evidence should move you: sample size, design, effect size, who chose the comparison, and what result would have been reported had it come out the other way.
nodes.why: Most disagreements about facts are actually disagreements about evidence weight, conducted without either side stating a weight.

evidence.measurementMethod: Given an unseen study or claim, state in advance how much it should move you and why; compare against a subsequent stronger source or replication.
evidence.knownLimitations: Evidence evaluation skill is real and teachable, but it is applied selectively: people evaluate evidence far more rigorously when they dislike the conclusion.

nodes.description: Establishing who is telling you something, what they know, what they gain, and what their track record is — before engaging with the content. The core move is lateral: leave the page and check the source elsewhere.
nodes.why: Reading a source carefully on its own terms is exactly how a well-constructed unreliable source wins. Checking sideways is faster and works better.

nodes.label: Causal Inference
nodes.description: Reasoning about what causes what, rather than what co-occurs: confounding, colliders, selection effects, and what intervention would distinguish the candidate structures.
nodes.why: Nearly every practical decision is a causal claim in disguise. Correlational literacy without causal structure produces confident, wrong policy.

evidence.measurementMethod: Given an unseen association, draw the causal graph, name the plausible confounders and colliders, and state the intervention or natural experiment that would settle it.
evidence.knownLimitations: Formal causal reasoning is teachable and the tools are well founded. Applying them to real observational data remains genuinely hard, and the assumptions are usually unverifiable.

nodes.label: Bayesian Updating
nodes.description: Moving a stated prior by a stated amount in response to evidence — including the discipline of writing the prior down before you see the evidence, so the update is visible.
nodes.why: Updating that is never quantified is indistinguishable from not updating, and both feel the same from the inside.

evidence.measurementMethod: Write a numeric prior, observe evidence, write a posterior, and later score the whole sequence against the outcome. Base-rate items in natural frequency format serve as a bench probe.
evidence.knownLimitations: Explicit Bayesian calculation improves reasoning on well-posed problems, especially in frequency format. It transfers poorly to messy real questions where the likelihood ratio is itself a guess.

nodes.label: Falsification & Disconfirmation
nodes.description: Actively seeking the observation that would show you are wrong, rather than accumulating observations consistent with being right. Operationally: naming the disconfirming test before gathering evidence.
nodes.why: Confirmation is the default and it is nearly free. The only reliable protection is deciding in advance what would change your mind, in writing.

evidence.measurementMethod: For each belief you test, did you specify a disconfirming observation in advance, and did you actually go and look for it? Wason-style rule-discovery items serve as a bench probe.
evidence.knownLimitations: Naive falsificationism is not how science actually proceeds — theories survive disconfirming results for good reasons. Treat this as a personal discipline, not a philosophy of science.

nodes.description: Constructing a comparison that can actually answer a question: controls, randomisation, sample size, pre-registered outcome, and the analysis decided before the data arrives.
nodes.why: A badly designed experiment is worse than none, because it produces a number that feels like evidence.

evidence.measurementMethod: Design an unseen study to a stated question and have the design critiqued for confounds, power and analytic flexibility — ideally by someone who did not help build it.
evidence.knownLimitations: Design skill transfers reasonably well across domains, but power analysis and measurement validity remain domain-specific and are where most real designs fail.

evidence.knownLimitations: This is a genuinely hard capability with very little training literature. Neuron includes it because its absence is catastrophic, not because the evidence for training it is good.

nodes.label: Expected Value
nodes.description: Weighing outcomes by their probability rather than by their vividness, and doing the arithmetic explicitly enough that someone else could check it.
nodes.why: The main benefit is not the number. It is that writing the terms down exposes which probability or payoff you were quietly refusing to state.

evidence.measurementMethod: Write the EV calculation before deciding, then score the process against the outcome — separately, because a good decision can lose.
evidence.knownLimitations: Expected value assumes your utility is linear in the units you chose, which it usually is not for large or irreversible stakes. Never apply it to ruin risk without a survival constraint.

nodes.label: Opportunity Cost
nodes.description: Pricing a choice by the best alternative it displaces rather than by its own merits in isolation. The operative discipline is naming the specific alternative, not gesturing at 'other things'.
nodes.why: Every yes is a no to something unstated. Making the displaced option concrete is what turns a plausible commitment into a comparable one.

evidence.measurementMethod: For each significant commitment, is the displaced alternative named specifically and in advance? Later, was it a better use of the same resource?
evidence.knownLimitations: People systematically under-generate alternatives, so the named alternative is often not the best one. Opportunity-cost reasoning improves comparisons; it does not fix a poor option set.

nodes.label: Decision Calibration
nodes.description: Making your stated confidence match your actual hit rate: when you say 70%, you are right about 70% of the time. Measured by scoring rules over many predictions, never by one.
nodes.why: Calibration is one of the very few cognitive properties that is objectively measurable at the individual level, improvable with feedback, and directly useful.

evidence.measurementMethod: Brier score and a calibration curve over your resolved predictions, decomposed into calibration and resolution so that hedging everything at 50% does not look like skill.
evidence.knownLimitations: Calibration is domain-specific and needs volume: fewer than about thirty resolved predictions tells you almost nothing. Being well calibrated is not the same as being knowledgeable.

nodes.label: Decision Journaling
nodes.description: Recording, at the moment of choosing, what you decided, what you expected, and what would tell you it was wrong — so that later review compares against the record rather than against memory.
nodes.why: Hindsight rewrites your prior beliefs silently and completely. Without a contemporaneous record you cannot learn from your own decisions at all.

evidence.knownLimitations: The habit is well argued and thinly evidenced. Its main established mechanism — defeating hindsight bias — is solid; broader claims about decision quality are not.

nodes.description: Deciding whether more information is worth its cost — which requires knowing whether the information could actually change the decision. Information that cannot change your action has zero value regardless of how interesting it is.

evidence.measurementMethod: Before investigating, state which answer would change your action and by how much; afterwards, check whether it did.
evidence.knownLimitations: Formal value-of-information analysis is well founded but demanding. The informal version is trainable; the quantitative version rarely survives contact with real uncertainty.

nodes.label: Reversibility & Optionality
nodes.description: Classifying decisions by how expensive they are to undo, and spending deliberation in proportion. Reversible choices deserve speed; irreversible ones deserve the slow path and a survival constraint.
nodes.why: Treating every decision as equally weighty is exhausting and slow; treating them as equally light is how people walk into unrecoverable positions.

evidence.measurementMethod: Classify decisions before making them and check afterwards: were the ones you called reversible actually reversed cheaply when they went wrong?
evidence.knownLimitations: The reversible/irreversible split is a useful heuristic with essentially no controlled evidence. People also systematically underestimate the cost of unwinding decisions they made quickly.

nodes.label: Divergent Generation
nodes.description: Producing many genuinely distinct options rather than variations on the first one. The measurable part is not fluency but distance: how different are options five through twenty from option one.
nodes.why: Option sets are almost always too small, and the first idea anchors every subsequent one. Deliberate generation is the cheapest fix available.

evidence.measurementMethod: Count distinct categories represented in an option set, not raw idea count; have someone else judge whether the last five are really different from the first.
evidence.knownLimitations: Divergent-thinking scores are trainable but their relationship to real creative achievement is modest, and creativity is substantially domain-specific. Group brainstorming reliably produces fewer ideas than the same people working alone.

evidence.knownLimitations: Reframing is easy to perform and hard to verify. Without a downstream test it produces the pleasant sensation of insight without any change in outcome.

nodes.description: Treating tool output as a claim requiring proportional checking: knowing which outputs are load-bearing, what an independent check would look like, and resisting the fluency of a confident answer.
nodes.why: Tools fail quietly and plausibly. The cost of a wrong answer you did not check scales with how much you trusted it, which is exactly backwards from how checking effort is usually allocated.

evidence.measurementMethod: Detection rate on deliberately seeded errors in tool output, and whether your checking effort tracked the stakes rather than your suspicion.
evidence.knownLimitations: Cognitive forcing functions reduce overreliance in controlled studies but cost time and are unpopular with the people using them. Sustained skepticism is expensive and fades.

nodes.label: Difficulty Calibration
nodes.description: Choosing practice that sits at the edge of your ability — roughly where you fail often enough to learn but not so often that you cannot recover. Includes tolerating the discomfort that signals it.
nodes.why: Difficulty selection determines the return on every hour of practice. Most self-directed practice sits far too easy because easy practice feels productive.

evidence.measurementMethod: Success rate at your chosen difficulty. Sustained accuracy well above about 85% means you are training too easy; chronic accuracy below about 50% means the task is not teaching.
evidence.knownLimitations: The optimal difficulty band is task-dependent and has no single universal value. Desirable difficulties reliably depress performance during practice, which makes adherence the real obstacle.

nodes.label: Feedback Integration
nodes.description: Converting feedback into a changed next attempt. The bottleneck is rarely receiving it — it is translating a comment into a specific behavioural difference and then actually making it.
nodes.why: Feedback that does not change the next repetition is entertainment. The translation step is the skill.

evidence.measurementMethod: For each piece of feedback: was a specific change named, was it made, and did the next attempt differ measurably?
evidence.knownLimitations: Roughly a third of feedback interventions make performance worse, particularly when feedback targets the self rather than the task. More feedback is not automatically better.

nodes.label: Practice Design
nodes.description: Designing the session itself: what to isolate, in what order, spaced how, with what feedback and what retention check. Practice design is the difference between hours logged and skill acquired.
nodes.why: Most people's practice is an inherited routine nobody examined. Designing it deliberately is a compounding advantage across every other node here.

evidence.measurementMethod: Retention and transfer tested at least a day after the session — never in-session performance, which is systematically misleading.
evidence.knownLimitations: The principles (spacing, interleaving, retrieval, variability) are well supported in aggregate; the optimal parameters for your specific skill are not known and must be found empirically.

nodes.label: Error Classification
nodes.description: Sorting your mistakes by cause — missing knowledge, wrong procedure, attention lapse, misread problem, or a genuine gap in understanding — because each demands a completely different fix.
nodes.why: Undiagnosed errors get the default treatment: more repetitions. That fixes one error class and wastes time on the other four.

evidence.measurementMethod: Whether the fix you applied actually eliminated that error class, checked on the next set of attempts rather than assumed.
evidence.knownLimitations: Self-diagnosis of error cause is unreliable, particularly for understanding gaps, which tend to be misclassified as carelessness. External review substantially improves classification accuracy.

nodes.label: Strategy Selection
nodes.description: Choosing the right learning strategy for the material at hand — and noticing when the one you are using has stopped working — rather than applying a single favourite technique to everything.
nodes.why: Strategy fit matters more than strategy quality. Spaced retrieval is excellent for facts and a poor fit for a motor skill or an unfamiliar proof.

evidence.measurementMethod: Track which strategy you chose, for what material, and what the delayed retention was. Over time the pattern is the measurement.
evidence.knownLimitations: Learners are poor judges of which strategy is working, systematically preferring the one that feels fluent. Without delayed testing this node trains preference, not selection.

nodes.label: Goal Decomposition
nodes.description: Turning a distant outcome into the nearest action that provably advances it, through a chain where each level is checkable. Distinct from planning: this is about the vertical chain from outcome to action, not the horizontal order of steps.
nodes.why: Goals fail at the level where 'become a better writer' meets Tuesday morning. Decomposition is what makes the abstraction actionable and, crucially, falsifiable.

evidence.measurementMethod: Can you name today's action and trace it upward to the outcome without a gap? Check monthly whether the completed actions moved any measurable outcome.
evidence.knownLimitations: Decomposition assumes the path is knowable in advance. For genuinely novel goals the chain is a hypothesis, and treating it as a plan produces confident motion in a wrong direction.

nodes.label: Prioritization
nodes.description: Ordering commitments by expected contribution under a real constraint, and saying no to the rest explicitly rather than by neglect.
nodes.why: An unordered list of good things is not a plan. Priority only exists where something was actually dropped.

evidence.measurementMethod: Did the top-ranked item actually receive the most attention this week? Compare your stated ranking against your calendar.
evidence.knownLimitations: Prioritisation frameworks proliferate and none has good comparative evidence. The measurable part is the gap between stated and enacted priority, which is worth tracking regardless of framework.

nodes.label: Scenario Planning
nodes.description: Building several internally consistent futures rather than one forecast, then identifying the decisions that hold up across all of them and the signals that would tell you which world you are in.
nodes.why: Point forecasts of complex systems are usually wrong. Scenario sets convert unpredictability into a decision structure instead of a prediction problem.

evidence.measurementMethod: Did the realised future fall inside your scenario set, and did the early indicators you named actually fire before it became obvious?
evidence.knownLimitations: Scenario planning has a long practitioner track record and little controlled evidence. It reliably broadens the option set; whether it improves decisions is not established.

nodes.label: Resource Allocation
nodes.description: Distributing time, attention and money across competing uses over a horizon longer than the current week, including the willingness to stop funding something that is not working.
nodes.why: Allocation, not effort, determines what a year produces. The hardest part is withdrawal from commitments that are merely acceptable.

evidence.measurementMethod: Planned versus actual allocation across categories, reviewed monthly, together with what you actually stopped funding.
evidence.knownLimitations: Personal allocation research is thin and largely borrowed from organisational finance. Sunk-cost effects are well documented and are the main failure mode here.

nodes.label: Strategic Thinking
nodes.description: Diagnosing a situation, choosing a guiding approach, and committing coherent actions to it — including what you will not do. Strategy is a diagnosis plus a choice, not a list of aspirations.
nodes.why: Most things called strategy are goals with adjectives. The diagnosis is the part that does the work and the part that is usually skipped.

evidence.measurementMethod: Can a reader state your diagnosis, your guiding policy and your coherent actions from the document alone — and identify what you ruled out?
evidence.knownLimitations: Strategy quality is judged largely retrospectively, and successful strategies are indistinguishable from lucky ones without a counterfactual. Treat measurement here as weak.

links.mechanism: A plan is a sequence held against a goal. If the goal is not actively represented there is nothing for the sequence to be evaluated against.
Initiation failures are frequently goal-representation failures: the intention is intact but not currently active when the trigger arrives.
A specified first action is the single strongest predictor of whether a task starts; planning is what produces one.
Both load the same executive substrate in Miyake's factor structure: switching requires suppressing the previously active task set.
An explicit plan gives errors something to be detected against; without an expected state there is no discrepancy signal.
Detecting that the current approach is failing is the trigger that a set shift requires; undetected errors produce persistence.
Provenance sets the prior weight before content is examined at all, which is what makes lateral reading faster than close reading.
The size of an update is a judgement about the evidence's likelihood ratio; without evidence weighting the arithmetic is theatre.
Design quality is the largest single input to whether an observed association licenses a causal reading.
You cannot design a comparison that isolates a cause without first representing the causal structure you are trying to cut.
A design is only informative if some outcome would have counted against the hypothesis; specifying that outcome is the falsification step.
Explicit updating makes visible the cases where no parameter value fits, which is the signal that the model rather than the estimate is wrong.
Repeatedly failing to find a disconfirmer that the model predicts should exist is evidence about the model's domain of validity.
Expected value is only as good as the probabilities entered into it; uncalibrated inputs produce precise, wrong numbers.
Opportunity cost supplies the comparison baseline an expected-value calculation is implicitly measured against.
The value of information is defined as the change in expected value it produces; without the EV frame the question cannot be posed.
Calibration requires a contemporaneous record of stated confidence. Memory reconstructs prior beliefs toward the outcome.
The journal is what reveals, in aggregate, which of your decisions actually turned out to be cheap to unwind.
Both answer the same question from opposite ends: how much deliberation this decision deserves before acting.
Selection is only meaningful over an option set that contains genuinely different options; otherwise it ranks variations of one idea.
Changing the problem statement changes which options are even generable — reframing expands the space that generation then searches.
Both depend on retrieving remote associates; the difference is that combination supplies a procedure for doing it deliberately.
Iteration needs a chosen candidate to iterate on. Without selection, cycles restart rather than converge.
Each cycle's failure is evidence about which constraint is actually binding, which is the input reframing needs.
A well-cut sub-problem is a searchable query. Most failed searches are searches for an undecomposed question.
Independent verification requires being able to find a second source that does not share the first one's inputs.
Delegation quality is bounded by specification quality; an undecomposed task cannot be handed to a tool or a person.
Without independent checking, assistance improves output inside the model's competence and degrades it outside, while confidence rises in both cases.
links.conditional: Matters most when the task sits near the boundary of the tool's reliable range.

links.mechanism: Writing the parts down is what makes their interfaces inspectable; decomposition held in the head collapses back into one blob.
Difficulty is the first parameter of any session design; every other choice is conditional on where the material sits relative to your ceiling.
A practice loop without a feedback channel is repetition. Designing the session means designing where the signal comes from.
Feedback is only actionable once the error's cause is identified; the same comment implies different fixes for different error classes.
You cannot compare strategies without holding session structure fixed enough for the comparison to mean something.
The distribution of your error causes is the main evidence for which strategy the material actually needs.
Ranking requires comparable units. Decomposition is what turns incomparable ambitions into candidate actions that can be ordered.
Allocation is prioritisation with a budget attached; an unranked list cannot be funded differentially.
A strategy that cannot be decomposed into this week's actions is an aspiration, and the decomposition attempt is what exposes that.
Scenarios identify which commitments are robust across futures, which is what a guiding policy needs to be built from.
Stated strategy and actual allocation diverge constantly; comparing them is the cheapest available audit of either.
The goal has to be held somewhere. Span sets the ceiling on how much context can stay active alongside the work itself.
Attention control and goal maintenance are measured by overlapping tasks and are plausibly the same capacity described from two directions.
Both load Miyake's shifting/updating factors, which are correlated but separable; a change in one predicts a partial change in the other.
The same suppression machinery, measured in an emotional and a neutral context; the correlation between the two is real but modest.
Implementation intentions work by pre-committing the trigger, which removes the decision that initiation usually stalls on.
Bias correction can only fire on a detected discrepancy; error monitoring supplies the discrepancy signal at the decision point.
Both build action structure from an outcome; planning orders steps horizontally, decomposition descends levels vertically.
Novel problems are solved by search, and planning is what keeps the search from re-exploring branches already ruled out.
Updating requires the probability machinery to operate on: priors, likelihoods and the conditioning step itself.
Establishing provenance means reading around a source quickly and accurately, which is analytical reading applied sideways.
Most evidence arrives as statistics. Misreading an interval or a base rate is the commonest evidence-weighting failure.
You cannot look for a disconfirmer until there is a specific hypothesis that predicts something could fail to appear.
A design is a hypothesis with a comparison attached; the hypothesis has to exist and be discriminating first.
Induction proposes the regularity; causal inference asks what structure could produce it and what else that structure implies.
Confirmation bias is the specific failure falsification discipline is built to counter, and naming it is the first step in the debiasing procedures that work.
Systems diagrams and causal graphs are the same object drawn by different communities; each catches errors the other tolerates.
A model library is only safe if each entry carries its domain of validity; otherwise breadth increases the rate of confident misapplication.
Calibration is measured with proper scoring rules over stated probabilities; the probabilities have to be meaningful first.
Payoff terms usually have to be estimated rather than looked up, and an order-of-magnitude error there dominates everything else in the calculation.
Expected value is arithmetic over quantities you must first read correctly out of the world.
The journal's main documented benefit is defeating hindsight bias, which requires knowing that hindsight bias is what is happening.
Recording expected outcomes is metacognitive monitoring with a timestamp attached.
Preserving optionality is only useful if you will actually switch when the evidence arrives; flexibility is what cashes the option in.
Combination requires mapping structure from one concept onto another, which is analogical mapping with the conclusion left open.
Both are fluency tasks over a constrained space; the difference is whether the output is judged for truth or for usefulness.
Imagining the hybrid object concretely is how its emergent properties become inspectable rather than merely asserted.
Improvisation is real-time divergent generation under a hard time constraint; the analogy is instructive but transfer between them is unevidenced.
links.conditional: Treat as a teaching bridge, not as a claim that practising one trains the other.

links.mechanism: Both are the discipline of pricing what you give up; one names the discarded option, the other names the displaced use of a resource.
A note system is external cognition specialised for retrieval over long horizons; the offloading mechanism is identical, the timescale is not.
Recognising that a task exceeds capacity is what prompts offloading; without load awareness the scratch pad never comes out.
Search is mostly rapid triage of candidate sources, which is analytical reading executed at low resolution and high speed.
Decomposition is the explicit content of algorithmic practice, and it is one of the few things from that practice that shows up outside it.
Domain fluency is what lets you see the jagged edge: without it, plausible wrong output and correct output are indistinguishable.
Automation bias is a specific, named failure mode; checking behaviour improves when the person expects it in themselves.
Offloading is valuable precisely because span is fixed; the size of the benefit tracks how far the task exceeds capacity.
Choosing difficulty requires an accurate read of your current ceiling, which is exactly what metacognitive monitoring supplies.
Retrieval is the best-evidenced component available to a session design; a design that omits it is leaving the largest known effect on the table.
Spacing is a scheduling parameter of the session design rather than a separate activity.
Interleaving is an ordering decision inside the session, and the one learners most reliably get wrong when left to themselves.
Integration requires feedback to exist. Seeking is upstream of using, and is the step most often skipped.
Classifying your own error causes is a monitoring judgement, and it inherits monitoring's known inaccuracy.
Strategies that vary context and require abstraction are the ones associated with transfer; selection is where that gets chosen or not.
Desirable-difficulty effects were established in motor learning first; the same manipulation reappears with the same signature there.
A ranking needs a criterion. Where the criterion is unstated, priority defaults to whatever is most urgent or most socially visible.
Scenarios have to be internally consistent, which means tracing feedback loops rather than varying one factor at a time.
Historical cases are the main source of scenarios that are not simply the present extrapolated, though the analogies mislead as often as they help.
Allocation over long horizons requires tolerating a worse near-term position, which is the delay choice with a spreadsheet attached.
Strategy defines the reservation value a negotiation defends; negotiation outcomes are the evidence that a strategy is or is not achievable.
Novel problems are attacked by reduction to solved sub-problems, which is decomposition doing the work under another name.
Speed–accuracy trade-off: pushing decision speed past your threshold degrades calibration well before it degrades felt confidence.
links.conditional: Only under time pressure. At a moderate pace the two are effectively independent.

links.conditional: During the generation phase only — inhibition helps during selection.

links.mechanism: Automatised responses execute below the threshold at which errors are consciously detected, so fluency lowers the self-catch rate.
links.conditional: Applies to the specific automatised mapping, not to your monitoring in general.

links.mechanism: Offloading generation removes the retrieval practice that builds depth — the Google effect applied to a skill rather than a fact.
links.conditional: Only when the offloaded task is one you are still trying to learn.
